cards.front: Recall a key point about Asteroids, Comets & Meteoroids
cards.back: Asteroids are rocky/metallic bodies, mostly found in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter

cards.front: Recall a key point about Asteroids, Comets & Meteoroids
cards.back: Comets are icy bodies that develop a coma and tail when they approach the Sun

cards.front: Recall a key point about Asteroids, Comets & Meteoroids
cards.back: A comet has a nucleus (solid core), coma (gas/dust cloud) and two tails: ion tail (pointing directly away from the Sun) and dust tail (curved)

cards.front: Recall a key point about Asteroids, Comets & Meteoroids
cards.back: Short-period comets originate from the Kuiper belt; long-period comets from the Oort cloud

cards.front: Recall a key point about Asteroids, Comets & Meteoroids
cards.back: Meteoroids are small rocky/metallic bodies in space; meteors ('shooting stars') are the visible streaks when they enter the atmosphere; meteorites are fragments that reach the ground

cards.front: Recall a key point about Asteroids, Comets & Meteoroids
cards.back: Notable asteroids include Ceres (also a dwarf planet) and Vesta

cards.front: What should you know about gcse astronomy exam tips — asteroids, comets & meteoroids?
cards.back: 1. For Asteroids, Comets & Meteoroids questions, define key terms before explaining processes 2. Use 'because' to link cause and effect in your explanations 3. Include units in all calculations and show your working for method marks 4. When evaluating Asteroids, Comets & Meteoroids, consider both the quality of evidence and practical implications 5. For extended response questions, plan your answer: identify AO1/AO2/AO3 requirements first

cards.front: Understanding Asteroids, Comets & Meteoroids in GCSE Astronomy
cards.back: Asteroids, Comets & Meteoroids is a key topic in GCSE Astronomy (AQA 8463 / Edexcel 1AS0) that requires understanding of both observational astronomy and theoretical concepts. You must be able to describe astronomical phenomena, explain the physical processes behind them, and apply mathematical relationships to solve astronomical problems.
